meta.descriptionEn: On 11 November 2000, 162 people boarded a modern funicular in the Austrian Alps for a morning of skiing on the Kitzsteinhorn glacier. Minutes later the train stopped inside a long mountain tunnel. What happened next turned an engineering marvel into the deadliest rail disaster in Austrian history. How could a small hydraulic leak and a heater built for homes bring down a system designed to be safe? Why could nobody call for help, and why did a handful of people survive by choosing the opposite direction? Follow the minute-by-minute story, the official inquiry, the courtroom verdicts and the safety lessons that followed.

articleEn: On the morning of 11 November 2000, a funicular train in the Austrian mountains set off carrying skiers toward the glacier. Just eight minutes later, 600 metres into the tunnel, it suddenly stopped. Then a fire began that no one could stop. In the disaster, 155 people died. Most of them were skiers heading for a holiday on the Kitzsteinhorn glacier. It is still regarded as the deadliest rail disaster in Austria's history.
This story is not only about a fire. It is about a train that turned into a chimney inside a mountain, and about questions whose answers took years to find.

The first question: how did the fire start? What happened on an ordinary train that changed everything within minutes? The second: why could people not get out? What roles did the doors, the windows and the design of the tunnel play? The third and most important: what changed afterward? Were those responsible identified, and did we learn any lessons?

In this article we look at the investigation report, go through the events of the disaster minute by minute, and learn the outcome of the court cases. First, let us go to the mountain where the journey began, because the story is incomplete without knowing the place.

articleEn: Many people hear the name Kaprun and think of the disaster. But the place is more than that: it is also a magnificent snow-covered mountain called the Kitzsteinhorn. It lies in Austria's High Tauern range, part of the Central Eastern Alps, and belongs to the Glockner Group. It is 3,203 metres high, and its glaciers are very popular with skiers. The mountain lies north of the Alpine crest, within the Kaprun municipality in the state of Salzburg.

Its summit was first climbed in 1828 by a local mountain guide, Johann Entacher. Skiing began here in the early twentieth century. Between 1907 and 1909 the German and Austrian Alpine Club built a mountain hut called the Krefelder Hütte. In December 1965 the first cable car began running, giving access to the Schmiedingerkees and Maurerkees glaciers. This created the first glacier ski slope in the Austrian Alps, an important step in the area's skiing history.

Reaching the summit is easy even today. The Glacier Aerial Tramway runs from the valley station, which stands 911 metres above sea level. On its route is the world's tallest cable car pylon, 113.6 metres high and 2.2 metres in diameter. The top station, at 3,029 metres, has a restaurant and a panoramic roof terrace.

There is also a problem. Since 1850, glaciers around the world have been retreating, and this resort is dealing with the effects of the environment too. Some scientists have measured a loss of more than two thirds of the glacier's surface area between the first detailed studies in the 1960s and 2022.

Now let us go back to 1974. Alongside the cable car, another route was built inside the mountain so that more people could reach the glacier. It was an underground funicular railway. Building its tunnel took two and a half years, and the tunnel was 3,295 metres long. Its purpose was to carry more passengers up the mountain. On this same funicular the disaster of 11 November 2000 took place. So what exactly is a funicular, and how does it work? We look at that next.

articleEn: A funicular is a cable railway system that connects different points of a railway track built on a steep slope. The word comes from the Latin funiculus, meaning rope, and the rope really is the heart of the whole system. Two carriages are permanently attached to the two ends of a haul rope, which passes over a pulley at the top. As a result, when one carriage goes up, the other comes down at the same speed, and the two counterbalance each other's weight.

That is why the engine only has to lift the extra passengers and the cable, plus the energy lost to friction. This is its great advantage, and it differs from an inclined elevator, which has just one car that is pulled upward. In most modern funiculars the carriages have no engine of their own. An electric motor turns a bullwheel through a gearbox, and the bullwheel drives the haul rope. The engine room has two sets of brakes, an emergency brake and a service brake. The carriages also carry rail brakes for emergencies. These rail brakes are applied by springs and released by hydraulic pressure. Remember this, because it becomes very important later in the story.

There are three main track layouts: four rails, three rails and two rails. In the two-rail layout both carriages share nearly the same track, with a passing loop in the middle where they pass each other. Its advantage is that it is the narrowest and needs only one platform at each station. But building the passing loop is more complex and more expensive.

Funiculars have a long history. The first line in Lyon opened in 1862, and Istanbul's Tünel has run continuously since 1875. In America, the Monongahela Incline in Pittsburgh opened to passengers on 28 May 1870. It is still the oldest and steepest continuously operating funicular there.

Some funiculars are quite unusual. Switzerland's Stoosbahn, with a 110 percent slope, is described as the world's steepest funicular. Haifa's Carmelit, with a tunnel 1.8 kilometres long, is technically an underground funicular, and Guinness World Records recognises it as the shortest metro.
So the principle is simple: one rope, two carriages and strong brakes. But the Kaprun 2 trains also had on-board hydraulic and electric systems. Let us look at them closely.

articleEn: The Kaprun 2 funicular ran from Kaprun to the Kitzsteinhorn. It opened in 1974 and was an important route for skiers heading to the glacier. Building its tunnel took two and a half years. The tunnel ran alongside the cable car so that more people could go up at the same time. In 1993 the funicular was modernised. The new systems installed seven years before the disaster would later prove very significant.

Now for the numbers. The whole line was 3,900 metres long, of which 3,300 metres were inside the tunnel. The track gauge was only 946 millimetres, an unusual width. It was a narrow track laid along the mountain slope. The slope was 30 degrees, and the train ran at 25 kilometres per hour. Most of the journey was inside the mountain.

The line had a single track, yet two trains ran at the same time. One went up while the other came down. In the middle was a section where the two trains passed each other, known as the passing section. The top of the tunnel ended at the Alpincenter, the main reception centre, where a motorised winch pulled the trains.

Next, the on-board systems. The train had a low-voltage electrical system and carried a conductor. For the brakes and doors it had 160-litre hydraulic tanks, so both brakes and doors ran on the hydraulic system. The braking principle is also interesting: the cars had spring-applied emergency rail brakes, released by hydraulic pressure.

The train's structure was simple. It had four passenger compartments and one conductor's cab at each end. When the train changed direction, the conductor moved from one end cab to the other. Each train could carry 180 passengers, so many skiers could reach the top in a single trip.

According to funicular expert Professor Josef Nejez, the designers believed a fire could not start inside a funicular. The reason was that no such fire had ever happened before. The train also fully met the area's safety codes. But those codes did not mention the systems added in the 1993 upgrade. This gap would later prove very costly.

So on the morning of 11 November 2000, skiers were boarding the funicular to go to the Kitzsteinhorn glacier. What happened on this narrow track that morning? In the next section we follow the clock, minute by minute.

articleEn: On the morning of 11 November 2000, shortly after 9 o'clock, people were boarding the train at the lower station in Kaprun. The trip carried 161 passengers and one conductor. Most were skiers heading for the slopes of the Kitzsteinhorn glacier. With a capacity of 180, the train was nearly full with 161 passengers, and the journey was about to begin as usual.

The train departed at 9:02 AM. What followed lasted only a few minutes, but its effects lasted for years. The train was climbing the 30-degree slope inside the tunnel. Coming down on the same route was the second train, carrying just one passenger. Then, eight minutes later, something unexpected happened. The train suddenly stopped. This was not a station but a stretch of tunnel. It stopped 600 metres inside the tunnel. Another figure is also given: 1,132 metres from the lower station. The source does not explain the difference between the two figures, so we give both numbers.

According to investigators, hydraulic pressure dropped, so the brakes engaged, and the hydraulic doors could not work either. The train had not only stopped; its doors would not open. The people inside had no direct way out. Investigators also say the hydraulic oil itself burned easily and made the fire worse.

A few minutes later the train assistant reported the fire to the control centre. An attempt was also made to open the doors, but it failed. Think about it: a fire inside a tunnel, closed doors, and only one attempt to contact the control centre. The passengers had no other way out. There was no cellphone reception in the tunnel, and no intercom. So the passengers could not talk to the conductor or call emergency services.

Then another problem arose. A 16kV power cable ran alongside the track. The fire reached the cable and burned it. As a result, power went out across the whole ski resort. With the blackout, the train assistant's contact with the control centre was also cut. Now the voices of those inside could not reach the outside. All this happened in just a few minutes, but every minute inside the tunnel counted.

Later investigation showed that the fire had started from a fan heater in the conductor's compartment. How did that heater cause a fire? We will look at the answer in detail in the investigation section. For now, remember this: the train had stopped, the doors were closed, the power was gone, and smoke was beginning to spread through the tunnel. Now the people inside had to decide. Break a window? Go down? Or go up? In the next section, these decisions change everything.

articleEn: What was happening inside the train? Smoke was increasing, and people were looking for a way out. Some passengers tried to break the windows. But the windows were made of shatter-resistant acrylic, so they were not easy to break. Then twelve people from the rear of the train broke one window with a ski pole. That moment became the biggest turning point of their lives.

Among them was a man who had once been a volunteer fire fighter. On his advice they went downward. They passed by the fire, taking a path downward under the smoke. The decision looked dangerous, but it saved them. They were 10 Germans and two Austrians, twelve people in all who managed to escape alive from this train. It is also important that the twelve who survived were in the rear of the train.

For the rest of the passengers the situation was harder. Because of smoke and toxic gases, many lost consciousness. Meanwhile the train assistant unlocked the doors using the electric system. Then they could be forced open by hand. Those who were conscious started moving up the tunnel to get away from the fire. But that direction proved the most dangerous. On one side was the decision of those who went down; on the other, the decision of those who went up. Both groups had very little time, and there was no intercom to guide them.

Why? Because the tunnel was acting like a giant chimney. Picture a long, narrow channel laid out on a 30-degree slope. According to accounts, the tunnel had become like a blast furnace. It drew oxygen in from below and sent smoke, heat and fire upward. That is why all those who walked upward, and the train assistant, died in the disaster.

This is the saddest part of the story. Above the burning train, in the same tunnel, was the other train. Its only passenger and its train assistant also died because of the smoke. Smoke and hot air kept rising. Finally they reached the Alpincenter, which stood 2,500 metres above the burning train.

At the Alpincenter two workers were running away, and they warned the employees and customers. Then they left through an emergency exit. They left the exit doors open. This helped the chimney effect even more, and the centre began filling with smoke. Most people got out of the centre, and only four stayed inside. Firefighters arrived and managed to revive one of them. The other three could not be saved. So the disaster did not stay confined to the tunnel; it reached the Alpincenter above.

Now the big question: the train carried 161 passengers, so why could only twelve get out? Part of the answer lay in the train's design. It had no smoke detectors, no intercom, and its fire extinguishers were out of the passengers' reach. And how did the fire start in the first place? Could it have been prevented? articleEn: On 6 September 2001, the official inquiry report was released. It said the fire was caused by a leak in one of the train's hydraulic pipes. The leak sprayed oil into the air as a fine mist. The oil was atomized, and that proved dangerous. The oil then met a fan heater. The heater was installed in the conductor's compartment and was not made for use in a moving vehicle. According to the inquiry, the atomized oil ignited from this heater. It is possible that a technical fault made the unit very hot.

The heater was made by a German company, Fakir. It was a model for household use, and its manual clearly said it should not be used in transportation vehicles. The way it was installed was strange too. The heater was opened up, the rear part placed behind the console panel and the front part left in view, and then it was screwed back together. The manufacturer had not approved this modification. In other words, a household appliance ended up where it had no business being.

Once the fire started, the hydraulic fluid itself burned easily. It melted the plastic fluid lines, which gave the flames more fuel. Another point emerged as well. When hydraulic pressure fell, the brakes engaged, and the same loss of pressure made the hydraulic doors stop working. The train stopped, and the very system that stopped it also disabled the hydraulic doors. This made it hard for passengers to get out. Remember that the train had 160-litre hydraulic tanks that ran both brakes and doors. Two very important functions depended on one system.

But the problem was not just the heater. Investigators found several structural flaws in the train's construction, especially a lack of safety mechanisms. Every funicular unit had fire extinguishers. But they were in sealed attendants' compartments, far out of the passengers' reach. The train had no smoke detectors. There was no cellphone reception in the tunnel, and no intercom. This meant the passengers had no way to contact the attendant or emergency services. They were completely cut off inside the mountain.

Why did the designers think this way? According to funicular expert Professor Josef Nejez, the designers believed a fire could not start in a funicular cabin. The reason? Such a fire had never happened before. A danger was ignored because it had not yet occurred.

Then there is the question of the law. The train met the area's safety codes, but those codes did not cover the systems installed in the 1993 upgrade. articleEn: At 1 PM that same day, Salzburg's governor, Franz Schausberger, held a press conference. He said there was no hope of any survivors apart from those who had got out by themselves. That morning the burning of the 16kV cable had caused a power blackout across the whole ski resort and cut contact with the control centre. A three-day national mourning period was declared across the country. It was the deadliest rail disaster in Austria's history.

Five days later, on 16 November, the recovery of all the victims was complete. But the destroyed train was still inside the tunnel. On 30 January 2001 it was removed from the tunnel, about two and a half months after the disaster.

The survivors included the people who escaped from the Alpincenter, the one person the firefighters revived, and the 10 Germans and two Austrians who got out by going down from the train. The number 155 is not just a statistic. These were 155 lives, most of them skiers heading up to the glacier.

Now to those who did not return. Most were skiers, and some were well-known names in sport. Among them was 19-year-old German freestyle skier Sandra Schmitt, who was the reigning World Champion in Women's Dual Moguls at the time. Josef Schaupper also died in the disaster. He was a seven-time Deaflympic medalist, and his deaf skier companions died with him. These names remind us that on that day more than a train stopped. The dreams of many athletes ended in the same tunnel.

This was the same 3,900-metre line that had been opened in 1974 for greater capacity. The question now was its future, and the answer was clear. It was never reopened, and the following year a gondola lift took its place. Called Gletscherjet I, a 24-person funitel, it entered service on 23 December 2001. The next year, on 19 October 2002, Gletscherjet II also opened.

The old funicular's track stayed in place until 2011. Then the track and the supporting structure under the tunnel were removed, and the tunnel mouth was sealed. The Kitzsteinhorn is still known today as a popular ski area. But the memory of 11 November 2000 will always be tied to its slopes.

articleEn: The criminal trial began on 18 June 2002. The 16 accused included the management of Kapruner Gletscherbahnen AG and officials from the Ministry of Transport and TÜV. The company denied responsibility. On 19 February 2004, Judge Manfred Seiss acquitted all the defendants because the evidence of criminal negligence was insufficient. In September 2007, the public prosecutor decided that the company that made the heater was not responsible. So no one could be proven responsible at the criminal level.

In 2007, Ed Fagan's class action failed and ended in his personal bankruptcy. By 2008, a settlement of 13.9 million euros was agreed with 451 claimants. On 11 November 2004, the fourth anniversary, a memorial was opened. The stone structure holds 155 glass columns, each representing one victim.

So what lessons came from this disaster? The first is that safety codes leave a gap if they do not cover systems installed after an upgrade. The second is that a train running in a tunnel needs basic facilities such as smoke detectors, an intercom and fire extinguishers within passengers' reach.

Still, one question remains open. When the inquiry listed so many failings, why could no one be held responsible for criminal negligence in court? If you liked this video, please like and subscribe, and tell us in the comments what you think is the most important step to prevent such disasters.

shorts.titleEn: The Ski Pole That Opened a Way Out of Kaprun
shorts.text: ایک ski pole نے 12 لوگوں کے لیے راستہ کھول دیا۔ یہ کیسے ہوا؟ 11 November 2000 کو Kaprun کی funicular train tunnel کے اندر رک چکی تھی۔ دروازے hydraulic نظام سے چلتے تھے، اور وہ کھل نہیں رہے تھے۔ کھڑکیاں shatter-resistant acrylic کی تھیں، انہیں توڑنا آسان نہیں تھا۔ پھر train کے پچھلے حصے سے 12 لوگوں نے ایک ski pole سے ایک کھڑکی توڑ دی۔ ان کے ساتھ ایک شخص پہلے volunteer fire fighter رہ چکا تھا۔ اس کے مشورے پر وہ اوپر نہیں گئے۔ وہ نیچے کی طرف نکلے، آگ کے پاس سے گزر کر، دھوئیں کے نیچے سے۔ فیصلہ خطرناک لگتا تھا۔ آخر میں 10 Germans اور 2 Austrians اسی راستے سے باہر نکلے۔ لیکن باقی لوگوں کے سامنے کون سا راستہ تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek ski pole ne 12 logon ke liye rasta khol diya. Yeh kaise hua? 11 November 2000 ko Kaprun ki funicular train tunnel ke andar ruk chuki thi. Darwaze hydraulic nizam se chalte thay, aur woh khul nahin rahe thay. Khirkiyan shatter-resistant acrylic ki thin, inhein torna aasan nahin tha. Phir train ke pichhle hisse se 12 logon ne ek ski pole se ek khirki tor di. Un ke sath ek shakhs pehle volunteer fire fighter reh chuka tha. Us ke mashwaray par woh upar nahin gaye. Woh neeche ki taraf nikle, aag ke paas se guzar kar, dhuen ke neeche se. Faisla khatarnak lagta tha. Aakhir mein 10 Germans aur 2 Austrians isi raste se bahar nikle. Lekin baqi logon ke samne kaun sa rasta tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

How 12 people escaped the Kaprun funicular by breaking a window with a ski pole.
A short look at one decision made inside the tunnel on 11 November 2000.

shorts.titleEn: A Household Heater and the Kaprun Fire Report
shorts.text: ایک گھریلو fan heater اور 155 جانیں۔ کیا یہ ممکن ہے؟ 6 September 2001 کو سرکاری inquiry کی رپورٹ آئی۔ اس کے مطابق train کی ایک hydraulic pipe سے تیل لیک ہوا اور باریک پھوار بن گیا۔ یہ atomized oil ایک fan heater تک پہنچا اور بھڑک اٹھا۔ یہ heater جرمن کمپنی Fakir نے بنایا تھا اور گھریلو استعمال کے لیے تھا۔ manual میں صاف لکھا تھا کہ اسے transportation vehicles میں استعمال نہ کیا جائے۔ رپورٹ کے مطابق ممکن ہے کسی technical fault سے unit بہت گرم ہو گیا ہو۔ مزید یہ کہ train میں smoke detectors نہیں تھے، اور tunnel میں cellphone reception بھی نہیں تھی۔ یعنی ایک چھوٹی سی چیز کے پیچھے کئی خامیاں چھپی تھیں۔ لیکن کیا کسی کو ذمہ دار ٹھہرایا گیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek ghareloo fan heater aur 155 jaanein. Kya yeh mumkin hai? 6 September 2001 ko sarkari inquiry ki report aayi. Is ke mutabiq train ki ek hydraulic pipe se tel leak hua aur bareek phuhar ban gaya. Yeh atomized oil ek fan heater tak pohancha aur bhadak utha. Yeh heater german company Fakir ne banaya tha aur ghareloo istemal ke liye tha. Manual mein saaf likha tha ke ise transportation vehicles mein istemal na kiya jaye. Report ke mutabiq mumkin hai kisi technical fault se unit bohat garam ho gaya ho. Mazeed yeh ke train mein smoke detectors nahin thay, aur tunnel mein cellphone reception bhi nahin thi. Yani ek chhoti si cheez ke peechhe kai khamiyan chhupi thin. Lekin kya kisi ko zimmedar thehraya gaya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
What the 2001 official inquiry found about the cause of the Kaprun funicular fire.
A heater not meant for vehicles, and several safety gaps.

September 2007 mein public prosecutor ne kaha ke heater banane wali company bhi zimmedar nahin. 2007 mein Ed Fagan ki class action nakam rahi.
